Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:20: There is yet another aspect of fear, and it is when a person considers the good that the Creator, blessed be He, bestows upon him beyond his due, as the pious author of Chovot HaLevavot elaborated, peace be upon him (Gate of Trust, chapter 6) - that the Creator's good to man exceeds anything a person could do in his whole life, for all his days and nights would not suffice to repay a single one of the Creator's kindnesses to him, as will be explained further in the Gate of Love from what our Sages, of blessed memory, explained. And if a person sins while the Holy One, blessed be He, bestows good upon him, he is found to be consuming his merits in this world, and his merits diminish - as our father Jacob, peace be upon him, said (Genesis 32:11), "I am unworthy of all the kindnesses and all the truth [You have shown Your servant]"; and Rashi explained: "my merits have been diminished through the kindnesses and truth You have done for me; therefore I fear that since You made me this promise I have become sullied by sin, which may cause me to be delivered into Esau's hand" - to this point. And so said the Targum: "my merits have grown few," and so on. Therefore a person must feel shame and not be ungrateful for the good that the Creator, blessed be He, bestows upon him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:21: There is a third aspect that our Sages, of blessed memory, explained in the Sifrei, cited in the Yalkut (Yalkut Kohelet, remez 971), on the verse (Ecclesiastes 5:1), "for God is in heaven," and so on - in these words: "'for God is in heaven' - and who does not know that the Holy One, blessed be He, is in heaven and mankind is on earth? Rather, Solomon meant: so long as even the weakest of the weak is above, he prevails over the mighty; [if] the weak one is below and the mighty one of the mighty is above, how much more so! And so it says (Deuteronomy 32:6), 'is this how you repay the LORD?'" - to the extent relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:22: Through this passage we may explain a verse from the words of King David, peace be upon him (Psalms 47:3), "for the LORD Most High is awesome, a great King over all the earth." The intent, according to what this passage says - that one who is above prevails over the mighty ones who are below - is: "for the LORD Most High is awesome" - from His being Most High, one must fear Him; how much more so that He is "a great King over all the earth," meaning that He watches over every detail of the world; and He is called "King" because He judges the world with judgment, for the world stands only through judgment, and a person is judged every day, as our Sages, of blessed memory, explained (Rosh Hashanah 16a). This will be explained further at length, with God's help.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:23: There is a fourth aspect that Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in the Tikkunim (5b), concerning the fear that comes from shame of face, in these words: "the eighth degree in the fear of the LORD is that one should have shame of face - one who has shame of face will not commit a transgression that comes to hand, because of fear of the Holy One, blessed be He, as though the world were created through him; and therefore 'Bereishit' [contains] 'yarei boshet' [fear (and) shame] - behold, fear and shame are one and the same."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:24: And he said further on: "moreover, shame of face [leads] to the Garden of Eden, and brazenness of face to Gehinnom; and those who commit transgression with a high hand and have no shame of face before the Holy One, blessed be He - of whom it is said (Isaiah 6:3), 'the whole earth is full of His glory,' and of whom it is said (Proverbs 20:27), 'searching all the chambers of the belly, seeing the kidneys and the heart' - and humility is bound up with fear, as it is said (Proverbs 22:4), 'the reward of humility is the fear of the LORD' - one who has the fear of the LORD is brought thereby to humility, which is the supernal Shechinah, for the fear of the LORD is [like] a heel to her. And this is the degree of Moses, of whom it is said (Numbers 12:3), 'and the man Moses was very humble' - and because fear is [merely] a heel to her [humility], the masters of the Mishnah established that 'fear' is a small matter compared to Moses" - to the extent relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:25: We find, then, that one must fear and feel shame before the Shechinah that is before him, for "the whole earth is full of His glory," and not transgress any of His commandments, blessed be He. And so wrote the author of Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of the Service of God, chapter 5): the pious one said, "do not rebel against your Master while He watches over you."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:26: Now, the fear from this aspect is the fear of which Scripture says (Exodus 20:17 [20]), "so that His fear may be upon your faces, that you sin not." And so our Sages, of blessed memory, explained in the Mechilta, and likewise in Nedarim, chapter 2 (20a), in these words: "It is taught: 'so that His fear may be upon your faces' - this refers to shame; 'that you sin not' - this teaches that shame leads to the fear of sin; from here they said, it is a good sign for a person to be bashful. Others say: any person who feels shame will not quickly sin, and whoever has no shame of face, it is known that his ancestors did not stand at Mount Sinai" - to this point. They were compelled to say that this fear is shame, because it says "upon your faces," for fear itself is only in the heart, as explained above; and further, what is meant by "that you sin not" - is it because the fear will be upon their faces that they will not sin? For this reason both [opinions] examined the matter closely, and said that the fear which is shame upon the face brings one to the fear of sin.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:27: Shame is when a person, embarrassed by worldly matters before another person, is modest in his actions; and likewise, when spoken to, he feels embarrassed and does not look the person in the face - this indicates the awe of the sovereignty of the King of the world upon him, and likewise his speech is gentle. This is the matter of shame, and from it the fear of sin follows for him. And in the Tikkunim (136a): "faces reddened with shame, who have embarrassment from Heaven - these are the God-fearing" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:28: The matter of the fear of sin was explained by Rabbeinu Nissim, peace be upon him, in the Baraita of Rabbi Pinchas (Avodah Zarah 20b): "watchfulness leads to alacrity," and so on; and he said there, "holiness leads to the fear of sin, the fear of sin leads to humility," and so on. The explanation of "fear of sin" is that one fears sin as one fears an enemy - meaning this is an additional degree in a person, that fear should be so firmly fixed in his heart that he fears the sin itself and keeps himself far, far from it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:29: It seems to me that "fear of sin" means that one fears to sin because of the disgrace of the sin itself - for how could one sin before the King who is before him and bring before Him refuse and transgressions, which are a deficiency [kelipah] subtracted from holiness, from the language of (I Kings 1:21), "I and my son Solomon will be [regarded as] sinners [chata'im]."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:30: And in Ra'aya Meheimna (Ki Teitzei 278b) it is explained that the fear of sin is the supernal Mother, Repentance, in these words: "a commandment is the soul [nefesh], the spirit [ruach] is Torah, and therefore they established that study is not the essential thing, but action; and elsewhere they said, whoever's fear of sin precedes his wisdom, his wisdom endures, and whoever's wisdom precedes his fear of sin, his wisdom does not endure. The fear of sin is the supernal Mother, Repentance; wisdom is the supernal Father. When the small Heh, which is the commandment, precedes, the Torah, which is Vav, rests upon him; and when fear precedes wisdom, which is the supernal Heh, wisdom, which is Yud, rests upon him, and he is called 'son' - and from here, 'you are children to the LORD your God'" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:31: We find, then, according to this, that the shame a person feels at sinning on account of the Shechinah - which is the very thing explained in the Tikkunim - brings him to attain a higher degree, which is the fear of sin; and this is what is explained in the Tikkunim (5b): that fear is bound up with humility, for from this it follows that he becomes humble, so that he does not respond to his own disgrace even when disgraced - for he fears and is ashamed to answer back before the King who is before him, as with Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, of whom it is said (Numbers 12:3), "and the man Moses was very humble," as is explained there in the Tikkunim, in the passage we cited. And this is [the meaning of] (Proverbs 22:4), "the heel of humility is the fear of the LORD" - meaning that the final degree of humility is the fear of the LORD, just as the heel is the end of a person's body; and since it says that the end of humility is the fear of the LORD, it appears that there is a bond between them, that both should be joined as one, this being the end and that being the beginning - and the bond between them is certainly the fear that comes from shame of face.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 3:32: This aspect of fear is explained in the Zohar (Naso 145a), in these words: "Rabbi Yitzchak opened [with the verse] (Psalms 103:17), 'but the kindness of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting upon those who fear Him' - how great is fear before the Holy One, blessed be He, for within fear is humility, and within humility is piety! We find, then, that whoever has the fear of sin has them all, and whoever does not fear Heaven has neither humility nor piety" - to this point. The matter of the fear of sin will be explained further in the next chapter, with God's help.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:1: This chapter will explain how many aspects there are to the matter of the fear of sin. First, one must fear that no sin should come to his hand, even unwittingly - the reason being that since the soul is a fine, spiritual entity, emanated from a high place, anything with which a person becomes blemished, even unwittingly, darkens the soul - like the parable of one who spills a jug of oil or ink upon his white, clean garments, even unintentionally; the stain darkens that garment. Concerning this King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Ecclesiastes 9:8), "let your garments be white at all times, and let oil not be lacking on your head."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:2: And they were stringent about this, saying in the Tanchuma (Parashat Vayikra), cited in the Yalkut (Parashat Vayikra, remez 464), on the verse (Leviticus 4:2), "when a soul shall sin unwittingly" - in these words: "to what may this be compared? To two men who sinned against the king, one a commoner and one of the palace. Seeing that both had committed the same sin, he pardoned the commoner but gave the palace-dweller a formal sentence. The palace people said to him: both sinned the same sin - the commoner you pardoned, but the palace-dweller you sentenced! He said to them: I pardoned the commoner because he does not know the royal customs, but the palace-dweller stands with me every day and knows the royal customs, and [yet] he sins. So too: the body is the commoner - 'and the LORD God formed man [of dust from the ground]' (Genesis 2:7) - while the soul is the palace-dweller from above - 'and He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life' - and both sin; therefore Scripture expresses astonishment, 'when a soul shall sin.' What is meant by 'unwittingly, against any of the commandments'? To teach you that whoever sins unwittingly is as though he transgressed a commandment of the LORD [deliberately]. And so it says (Numbers 15:22), 'and when you shall err, and not observe all these commandments'; and it says (Psalms 19:13), 'who can discern his errors?... also keep back Your servant from willful sins' - an unwitting error in study amounts to willfulness" - to the extent relevant here. Here it is explicitly stated that the punishment falls upon the soul because it was the palace-dweller, a child of the chamber of the Supreme King, and knows the royal customs, which is the Torah that is taught to it before it comes into the world.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:3: As for what it says, "stands with me every day" - this refers to the fact that every night the soul ascends above to report on a person's deeds, as our Sages, of blessed memory, explained (Tanna Devei Eliyahu Zuta, chapter 1): "'she who lies in your bosom, guard the doors of your mouth' (Micah 7:5)" - and according to its merit, so it sees above and is taught, as we shall elaborate further on this, with God's help.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:4: One may also say that "stands with me" refers to engagement with Torah - that one who reads the Torah stands with the Holy One, blessed be He, in the manner explained by our Sages, of blessed memory (Tanna Devei Eliyahu Rabbah, chapter 18), on (Lamentations 2:19), "pour out your heart like water before the presence of the LORD": "one who reads and studies - the Holy One, blessed be He, sits opposite him and reads and studies with him," and so on; and from this he knows the royal customs. The first explanation, however, appears to me the primary one.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:5: According to this midrash, the body has no punishment. But there are those who disagree with it in Midrash Vayikra Rabbah (4:5), saying that the soul and the body are both punished together, and they bring, for this, the parable of the lame man and the blind man. And concerning this it is said (Psalms 50:4), "He calls to the heavens above, and to the earth, to judge His people" - "He calls to the heavens above" to bring the soul, "and to the earth" to bring the body, "and afterward, to judge His people." And so our Sages, of blessed memory, also explained (Sanhedrin 91b); it appears that this view is more widely accepted.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:6: Let us return to our subject: for it is proven from the words of the midrash that a person is punished in two respects. The first is because his soul is spiritual, a child of the King, and it was fitting for it to gaze upon the glory of the Supreme King; and even if he sinned unwittingly, he is punished as though he transgressed deliberately, because an unwitting error in study amounts to willfulness. And what is said, "and it says, 'and when you shall err, and not observe all these commandments'" - may be understood from what is explained in Ra'aya Meheimna, cited in Parashat Naso (124a), in these words: "and whoever fulfills a single commandment properly is as though he fulfilled all two hundred forty-eight positive commandments, for there is no commandment that does not comprise within it all two hundred forty-eight" - to this point. Now, from the [principle governing] fulfillment we may know the punishment for transgression: for one who transgresses a single commandment is as though he transgressed them all, and this is [the meaning of] "and when you shall err, and not observe all these commandments."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:7: And in the Zohar (Vayikra 13a), a passage bearing on our discussion is explained concerning this verse (Leviticus 4:2), "when a soul shall sin unwittingly" - and I have seen fit to cite it here, though it is long, because of its great benefit for the matter of fear and repentance; and it follows the same lines as what is explained in the midrash we cited. In these words: "'when a soul shall sin' - Rabbi Yosi opened [with the verse] (Song of Songs 2:17), 'until the day breathes and the shadows flee,' and so on. How much must people be careful of their sins, not to sin before their Master! For every single day a herald goes forth and calls: awaken, people of the world, and weep before the Holy King; awaken, be careful of your sins; awaken, O holy soul that was placed within you from a holy, supernal place! For we have learned that at the time the Holy One, blessed be He, brings forth the soul to descend into human beings, He makes it testify with many oaths, many bonds, to keep His commandments; and not only that, but He causes it to pass through a thousand and eight worlds to delight and to see there the glory of those who occupy themselves with Torah. It goes forth and stands before the King in a garment of honor, and afterward, in the image of this world, it gazes, in that supernal light, upon the King's glory every day, and He crowns it with many crowns. When the time comes for it to descend to the world, it makes its dwelling in the Garden of Eden for thirty days, to see the glory of the Master of the righteous, and it ascends to its place; and afterward it descends to the world. The Holy King crowns it with seven crowns, until it comes and enters the body of a person, and it returns [dwells] in this world and occupies itself with its darkness. The Torah is astonished at it and says: and all this glory, and all this perfection that the soul of the Supreme King has been granted, and it hides itself before Him - 'when a soul shall sin'? What is this, that it should sin? Rabbi Yosi said: 'when a soul shall sin' - I return to the verse 'until the day breathes' - this is counsel for this soul, to be careful of its sins and to repent and be purified before the day breathes - before this world's day breathes and that mighty day comes when the King demands judgment of it, to depart from this world."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:8: "And the shadows flee" - this is the secret that the Companions state: at the time when a person's time comes to depart from the world, the person's shadow departs from him; this is [the meaning of] "until the day breathes" - until the day breathes [its last] for him to depart from this world - "and the shadows flee," that the shadow departs, and he sits before his Master.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:9: Rabbi Elazar said: a person has two shadows while he is alive - one large and one small, and they are found together; thus is a person while alive. And therefore it is written "and the shadows flee" [plural] - for then a person must examine his deeds and set them right before his Master, and confess them, for the Holy One, blessed be He, is called merciful and gracious, and accepts those who repent before Him; and this is [the meaning of] "until the day breathes and the shadows flee" - for once those shadows depart from him and he is caught, as it were, in a collar, repentance [is still possible], but not as perfect as at the time when he is [fully] alive. King Solomon proclaimed and said (Ecclesiastes 12:1), "and remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come," and so on; and therefore, "until the day breathes" - a person must set his deeds in order, for when his days draw near to depart from the world, the Holy One, blessed be He, is astonished at him and says, "and when a soul shall sin" - "and it has heard the voice of adjuration" [Leviticus 5:1] - for I made it swear an oath by My Name not to be false to Me, and I made it testify when it descended into the world. And He is a witness - certainly, from the many times He made it testify to keep the commandments - and therefore, since a person is a witness [against himself] at the time he returns before the King, whether he has seen or known - whether he saw the sins he committed and considered them, or knew for certain that he transgressed the command of his Master - if he does not declare it, if he does not confess it before his Master, what is written concerning when he departs from this world? "He shall bear his iniquity" - and when he bears his iniquity, how will a gate be opened for him, and how will he stand before his Master? And therefore it is written, "when a soul shall sin" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:10: Behold, it is explained in this passage how greatly the Holy One, blessed be He, is astonished at the soul when it does not do the will of its Creator, because it stood above and saw the King's palace and its customs - and this follows the same lines as the first passage from the Tanchuma that we cited at the beginning of the chapter.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:11: In this manner it is further explained in a midrash cited in the Yalkut (Parashat Ha'azinu, remez 942), on the verse (Deuteronomy 32:2), "my teaching shall drip as the rain" - in these words: "and so Rabbi Simai used to say: all creatures created from the heavens, their soul and body are from the heavens; and all creatures created from the earth, their soul and body are from the earth - except for this man, whose soul is from the heavens and whose body is from the earth. Therefore, if man performs the Torah and does the will of his Father in heaven, he is like the beings above, as it is said (Psalms 82:6), 'I said, you are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.' If he does not perform the Torah and does not do the will of his Father in heaven, he is like the beings below, as it is said (ibid.), 'nevertheless, you shall die like men.' Rabbi Eliezer, son of Rabbi Yosi HaGelili, says: if the Angel of Death should come and say to me, why was I created? I would say to him: I was created for the sake of the nations of the world, should they not accept My Torah - not for My children" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:12: Further, regarding the punishment for an unwitting act, it is explained in the Talmud, tractate Nazir (23a), of blessed memory: "Similarly (Numbers 30:13 [Hebrew 30:9 similar; here Nazir 23a's referent]), 'her husband has voided them, and the LORD will forgive her' - Scripture speaks of a woman whose husband voided [her vow] and she did not know; [yet] she requires atonement and forgiveness. And when Rabbi Akiva would reach this verse, he would weep: if one who intended to bring up pork [in his hand] and it turned out to be lamb still requires atonement and forgiveness, how much more so one who intended to bring up pork and it turned out to be pork!" And further there: "Isi ben Yehuda says, 'and did not know, and is guilty, and shall bear his iniquity' (Leviticus 5:17) - over this matter, let all who grieve, grieve" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:13: Further, I found a passage of Tanna Devei Eliyahu speaking on the matter of fear, and I have seen fit to cite it here; it is printed in the Yalkut, Parashat Lech Lecha (remez 76), on the verse (Genesis 15:3), "and Abram said, behold, to me You have given no offspring," and so on - in these words: "a person should always guard in his heart against coming to sin, even a light sin. Go and learn from our first forefathers, who went down to Egypt only because of a light matter that Abraham said, 'how shall I know?' And as a reward for the small measure of fear that Ishmael showed his father, the Holy One, blessed be He, did not permit any nation or kingdom to rule over his children [completely]. And as a reward for the two tears that Esau shed, they gave him Mount Se'ir, from which the rains of blessing never cease. And as a reward for his taking his belongings and going away from his brother Jacob, they gave him a hundred provinces. And as a reward for Jacob's heeding Joseph, he was punished for it for twenty-two years. And because of strife, Moses and Aaron were punished. The Sages said: if fire has caught hold of the moist [wood], what will become of the dry? And concerning that time it says, 'a prayer of Moses'" [Psalms 90:1].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:14: The Holy One, blessed be He, then returned to appease Moses. He said to him: is it not I who said, "you are children [to the LORD your God]" - I am your Father; you are My brothers and I am your brother; you are My friends and I am your friend; you are My beloved and I am your beloved - have I withheld anything from you? I ask of you nothing but what I sought within Myself and found - eleven qualities - so I ask of you only eleven qualities, and these are they (Psalms 15:2), "he who walks blamelessly, and does righteousness," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:15: Again the Holy One, blessed be He, returned to appease Moses. He said to him: is there before Me any favoritism, whether gentile or Israelite, man or woman, servant or maidservant? Whoever performs a commandment, its reward is alongside it, as it is said (ibid. 36:7), "Your righteousness is like the mighty mountains," and so on. From here they said (Bamidbar Rabbah 4:20): whoever increases the honor of Heaven and diminishes his own honor - the honor of Heaven increases and his own honor increases; and whoever diminishes the honor of Heaven and increases his own honor - the honor of Heaven remains in its place, and his own honor is diminished.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:16: There was an incident concerning a man who was standing in the synagogue with his son standing opposite him; and while all the people were responding "Hallelujah" after [the reading of] the ark, his son was responding with idle words. They said to him: look at your son, who is answering with idle words! He said to them: what shall I do with him - he is a child, let him play. The next day he did the same, and throughout all eight days of the festival, and he said nothing to him. Before one year, or two years, or three years had passed, that man died, and his wife died, and his son died, and his son's son died, and fifteen souls went forth from his household, and only one pair remained to him - one lame and blind, the other a fool and wicked.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:17: Again, there was an incident concerning a man who used to regret that he had not read [Scripture] or studied [Mishnah]. Once he was standing in the synagogue, and when the one passing before the ark reached the sanctification of the [Divine] Name, he raised his voice and said, "Holy, holy, holy." They said to him: why did you raise your voice? He said to them: I did not merit [to learn] Scripture or Mishnah, and now that permission has been given to me [to say this], shall I not raise my voice, that my soul may find satisfaction? Before that year, or two, or three years had passed, that man went up from Babylonia to the Land of Israel, and they made him the general of Caesar's army, and appointed him head over all the fortresses in the Land of Israel, and gave him a place, and he built a city and settled in it, and it was called "Colonia" after him, for him and his children and his children's children forever.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:18: There was an incident concerning a certain priest who fed his animal terumah [priestly tithe], and fire fell upon him and consumed from him thirty stacks of grain, thirty garments, twenty-four jars of wine, sixteen jars of oil, and other property he had. He came and stood before the Sages and told them what had happened to him. He said to them: I am a priest, and I fed my animal terumah. The Sages heard and said: blessed is the Omnipresent, who shows no favoritism! For does not terumah and consecrated produce that have no eaters go only to be burned? He said to them: but did you not teach me that vetches of terumah may be fed to cattle, wild animals, and chickens? They said to him: they only permitted this regarding vetches which are, from the outset, animal food, and which people eat [only] in a year of famine - therefore David decreed concerning them [that they be treated more leniently]. From here they said: whoever feeds his animal terumah, even terumah from outside the Land, of him Scripture says (Proverbs 19:16), "he who despises his ways shall die," and it says (Numbers 18:32), "and you shall not profane the holy things of the children of Israel," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:19: We learn from Abraham that from the beginning of his deeds he feared before the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said (Genesis 15:1), "fear not, Abram" - for one says "fear not" only to one who truly fears Heaven. They gave a parable for this: to what may this be compared? To a king who said to his son, go forth and kill these bandits, and if they fall into your hand, do not benefit from their wealth, so that people should not say the king's son went forth to kill these bandits only to seize their wealth. He went forth and killed them; on his return, his father went out to meet him and said to him: my son, blessed are you, and may you have satisfaction of mind that you took no benefit at all from their wealth, and now I will pay you from my own treasury - silver, gold, precious stones, pearls, and every desirable object in the world. For this reason our father Abraham was compared [to this]: at the time he killed the kings, the king of Sodom went out to meet him and said to him, "give me the persons," and so on [Genesis 14:21]. He said to him: fool of the world! Do I need silver, gold, precious stones, pearls, and every desirable object of yours - from a thread to a shoelace [I will not take anything of yours]? For this reason it is said, "I am your shield," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:20: We learn from Isaac that from the beginning of his deeds he feared before the Holy One, blessed be He. Isaac was seventy-five years old at the time our father Abraham passed away. He said: woe is me, perhaps I do not have good deeds such as my father had - what will become of me before the Holy One, blessed be He? Immediately the mercy of the Holy One, blessed be He, was stirred, and He spoke with him that very night, as it is said (Genesis 25:11), "and it came to pass after the death of Abraham," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:21: We learn from Jacob that from the beginning of his deeds he feared Heaven, as it is said (ibid. 35:4), "and they gave to Jacob all the foreign gods," and so on. And likewise our first forefathers, as it is said (Exodus 14:31), "and Israel saw the great hand," and so on - to teach you that as a reward for the fear and the faith with which they believed in Him at first, the Holy One, blessed be He, will in the future come and redeem them, as it is said (Micah 4:10), "writhe and labor to bring forth, O daughter of Zion," and so on - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:22: Regarding the matter of the fear of sin, Rashbi, peace be upon him, further explained (Zohar, Bereshit 7b), in these words: "why is it called 'the fear of the LORD'? Because it [Malchut] is the Tree of Good and Evil - if a person merits, behold, good; and if he does not merit, behold, evil; and therefore fear rests in this place, and it is the gate above to all the good of the world" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:23: The intent of his asking "why is it called the fear of the LORD" is to raise two questions: first, concerning the very existence of fear in this place [Malchut]; and second, what is the connection to the two words "fear of the LORD," rather than saying "fear of God"? And he answered: "because it is the Tree of Good and Evil." My teacher, peace be upon him, explained, in his commentary on the Sabba, that this attribute [Malchut] is called the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil because it draws from the depth of good and the depth of evil, which are kindness and judgment; and further, that beneath it are good and evil, as is explained in the Tikkunim (90b): "the Tree of the Knowledge of good - this is Metatron; and evil - this is Samael." And Scripture says (Deuteronomy 30:15), "see, I have set before you today life and good, and death and evil" - life is bound with good, and death is bound with evil, and two paths branch out from it [Malchut] below, and therefore this is the place of [free] choice, and it is written, "and you shall choose life." And if a person merits through his deeds, he cleaves to the good, which is "the LORD," the Tree of Life, which is the side of kindness and mercy - namely (Psalms 145:9), "the LORD is good to all, and His mercies are over all His works" - and likewise "the LORD" [in gematria] adds up to "TOV" [good] with the kolel; and if he does not merit, he cleaves to the evil, which is death, namely the external husks [kelipot].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:24: With this both points of grammar are resolved: one must fear because beneath it is evil, lest his soul cleave to evil - for death and the evil to which it cleaves become the portion of his soul after his departure from the world, in the manner explained in the Zohar (Parashat Korach 177a), on the verse (Job 34:11), "for the work of a man He will render to him." And likewise, one should not cause this attribute [Malchut] to cleave to evil, Heaven forfend, as will be further explained concerning the blemish a person causes to the [divine] attributes, blessed be He. And likewise "the fear of the LORD" - for if one fears, he merits to cleave to "the LORD," which is good, and his soul, after its departure from the world, cleaves to the good - namely, the good that is hidden away for the righteous in the Garden of Eden - "and God saw the light, that it was good," for "the LORD" is the source of all the good in the world; and this he examined closely by saying, "this is the gate to enter into all the good of the world." And the word "good" follows the principle that "there is nothing higher than delight" [oneg]; also, the word "good" comprises all the good found in all the [divine] attributes, this being "the LORD," the totality of the ten attributes in direct light, which is kindness and mercy, as is explained in the Tikkunim (6b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:25: Now, man is composed of good and evil, which are the good inclination and the evil inclination; and if a person merits to subdue the evil inclination within him, he causes the subduing of the [forces of] judgment and the husks, and causes the drawing forth of good upon himself - and this is what is meant by the precise wording "if a person merits" - for a person is composed of good and evil, and must strengthen the good inclination over the evil inclination; and if, Heaven forfend, he does the opposite, he blemishes the supernal roots, for judgment is not comprised under kindness [when it dominates].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:26: This is explained in the Zohar (Va'era 26b), on the verse (Deuteronomy 4:39), "and you shall know this day, and take it to your heart" - in these words: "Rabbi Elazar further said: the wicked cause a blemish above. What is this blemish? That the left is not comprised within the right - that the evil inclination is not comprised within the good inclination, because of the sins of mankind; and the blemish they cause affects only themselves, as it is written (ibid. 32:5), 'He has become corrupted, not His children, the blemish is theirs' - as it were, they act, and yet they do not act: they act, so that the blessings from above are not drawn down upon them, as it is said (ibid. 11:17), 'and He will restrain the heavens, and there will be no rain'; and they do not act, for the heavens themselves take for themselves the blessings they need, and do not take them to draw them down below - and certainly the blemish belongs to those wicked ones. Further, [the word] 'lo' [not, spelled with a Vav in this reading] indicates that the right is not comprised within the left, so that blessings are not drawn down below; [the word] 'lo' [with an Alef, meaning 'to Him'] indicates that they do not take [the blessings] to draw them down below. Who causes this? Because the wicked separate the evil inclination from the good inclination and cleave to the evil inclination" - to the extent relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:27: Our intent in citing this is clear, but nevertheless let us explain the matter of the blemish he mentioned, "they act, and yet they do not act." The intent is that Rabbi Elazar found the plain sense of the verse difficult: for if, as it appears, "He has become corrupted, not" - meaning that no blemish reaches Him, blessed be He, from our deeds, but rather "His children, their blemish" - that the blemish and the flaw are in the children who commit that blemish and sin - if so, the verse should simply have said "His children, their blemish, a perverse and crooked generation," [without the intervening word]. Therefore he explained that the intent of "He has become corrupted" is that a blemish does reach Him, but it is not a complete blemish - this is [the meaning of] "lo" spelled with an Alef [merely "to Him," a partial effect]; but the complete blemish and flaw is in the children who commit it - "His children, their blemish" [mumam]. Therefore, regarding what pertains to Him, it says "shichet" [corrupted], which is a minor corruption, but what pertains to the children is a complete "mum" [blemish]. With this we may understand the words of Rabbi Elazar, peace be upon him, who said "the wicked cause a blemish above," and so on, and then said "and the blemish they cause affects only themselves" - that the actual blemish is in them.
